title: Barry Lyndon and a certain story moment

commenti.body: I recently picked up Barry Lyndon on sale and re-watched it.  I admit to being a fan and find the "boringness" part of the appeal.  There are a lot of dry funny moments in the movie, often through the incongruity of the narrator's PoV and the action happening on screen.  A moment that had me laughing pretty hard this last time was when Barry is being awarded a commendation from the Prussian army and the officer is dressing down what a vagrant and ne'er do well he must be.  Barry's exceedingly formal and passionate answer about going to Hell for the regiment is so funny when you're aware of how rootless and disloyal he is to every one he encounters.

One of the most funny scenes is when Barry gets mad at his stepson and starts beating him up. I think most directors would have shot this scene dramatically, since this is when Barry’s fate goes very downhill. But Kubrick goes for complete slapstick. He can see that it’s a bunch of guys in wigs who are slipping on the polish. He shoots it to parallel the scene where Barry has a fistfight in the army and everyone gets rowdy. It’s interesting how it helps show how violence permeates. 

I think it takes personality to put such a slapstick scene in your 3h30 period piece staged to follow classical music.

Yeah exactly the "boringness" is so comforting and makes it easier to fully absorb the visual beauty

Barry Lyndon is one of comfort films

Along with Satantango, curiously enough

Barry Lyndons most over arching theme is that life is an absurd adventure full of absurd plot twists but in the end no matter the risks you take and the luck you have, it can all come crashing down for circumstances out of your control. Or, if you become a narcissist, it can speed that demise.

Yes the joke landed for me. I love absurdist takes. A lot of people find the moral depressing. The key is to find the absurdist mindset liberating.

“It was in the reign of George III that the aforesaid personages lived and quarreled; good or bad, handsome or ugly, rich or poor they are all equal now.”

I accepted upon rewatching it again recently that it is absolutely intended as a comedy. I think the aesthetics obfuscate this fact. In the west we’re taught about the antiquity of European history with an air of reverence. That the art, the music, the politics, wars, etc- are all very Important, and should viewed as such. The film leans into this reverence. Relying heavily on grand architecture, sweeping classical music, and painterly lighting/frames. Yet at its core it’s a film about men in silly wigs standing perfectly still ten steps apart while they take turns blasting metal balls at each other. The aforementioned reverence actually adds to the comedy of these situations. The fact that everyone involved takes it all so seriously is itself a vehicle of comedy.

I love Barry Lyndon and it took me several failed attempts before I understood the humor and it became one of my favorite movies.  When I was around 20 and really getting into film I had only watched it at home on DVD and could not make it through.  It was just boring and slow to me, but I was still a huge Kubrick fan.  The opportunity to see one of his films on the big screen arrived and, to my disappointment, it was Barry Lyndon.  I decided to bear it so that I could see at least one SK film on a big screen while I had the chance.  Turns out the audience got the humor, and hearing them laugh turned a switch on in my brain.  It turned out to be one of the best 3:30h film experiences of my life.  I could see the majesty of the cinematography and how most of the shots were composed to resemble 19th century paintings.  Amazing film, and yes, I totally understood the moment of the film in question.  It was like his whole life was a lie and he had gone through all that anxiety, had been robbed, joins the military, and then finds out it was all a sham.

Barry Lyndon was a full-on comedy for me, I laughed like every five minutes. It's so absurd and a pretty brutal satire of the European aristocracy. The zoom-ins or zoom-outs are so frequently funny that I was never bored.

One of the funniest parts is also when Barry just steals the officer's uniform while he was bathing (or was it having an affair?). You can literally see the gears turning in Barry's head and then he just swipes the uniform and prances off so stoically...I cracked up.

There is a comic undertone throughout, but my question is how much of this is Thackeray and how much is Kubrick. Thackeray was writing in the much more subdued and serious 1840's after the Victorian reaction against the baroque extravagances of the Georgian and Regency periods. I have always assumed that Thackery was writing social satire but I have never read the book.

I thought it was somewhat amusing but I mostly felt the impact of it only in the sense of it being a social commentary. That a family of this era will do anything in order to the avoid the humiliation of poverty. I think Lyndon is a great film overall but as with much of Kubrick's work, I don't get emotionally attached to it.

So glad to see this is top comment. I think this is one of the funniest scenes in a film ever.

It's like a joke whose set-up takes 2+ hours; every camera movement is so staid and painterly, then you have just an absolute explosion of chaos that feels so disruptively hilarious, and it's done with nothing but hand-held shaky cam. 

One of the best cinematic effects in the film, and it's used for laughs.
